blocks.title: Nutrients
blocks.md: **Nutrients** are the substances in food that the body uses. The main groups are **carbohydrates**, **fats**, **proteins**, **vitamins**, **minerals**, **water** and **fibre**. Carbohydrates, fats and proteins are needed in larger amounts and are called **macronutrients**.

blocks.title: Carbohydrates and fats
blocks.md: **Carbohydrates** (starches and sugars) give energy. Sources: cassava, plantain, maize, rice, yams, cocoyam, bread. **Fats and oils** give a concentrated supply of energy, protect organs and carry some vitamins. Sources: palm oil, groundnut oil, groundnuts, butter, fatty fish.

blocks.caption: A table with carbohydrate, fat and protein, their main job and an example food.
blocks.alt: Table of three nutrients with their job and a food example.

blocks.title: Proteins
blocks.md: **Proteins** are for **growth and repair** of the body (they can also give energy). Sources: fish, meat, eggs, milk, beans, groundnuts, soya, crayfish. Proteins from animals and plants can be combined in a meal, for example beans with maize or plantain.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- 'Energy foods' means mainly carbohydrates and fats.
- Too much sugar and fat is not healthy; keep a balance.
- Do not say a single food gives everything the body needs. Health information here is general and flagged for review.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Classify these local foods by their main nutrient: plantain, beans, palm oil.
steps: Plantain is mainly starch, a carbohydrate.
Beans give protein; palm oil is a fat/oil.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A child in Buea is growing fast. Which nutrient is especially important and which foods could supply it?
steps: Examples: fish, eggs, beans, groundnuts (according to what the family can afford).

blocks.title: Vitamins and minerals
blocks.md: **Vitamins** and **minerals** are needed in small amounts to keep the body healthy. **Vitamin A** helps sight and the skin; **vitamin C** helps the body heal and resist infection; **vitamin D** helps bones (the body also makes it with sunlight); **iron** helps make blood; **calcium** builds bones and teeth; **iodine** helps the thyroid gland.

blocks.title: Sources
blocks.md: Vitamin A: orange and green leafy vegetables, red palm oil, liver, eggs. Vitamin C: oranges, guavas, mangoes, pawpaw, tomatoes and fresh vegetables. Iron: meat, fish, beans, green leaves. Calcium: milk, small fish eaten with bones, green leaves. Iodine: fish and iodised salt.

blocks.caption: A table pairing four nutrients with food sources.
blocks.alt: Table: vitamin A with palm oil and green leaves, vitamin C with orange and guava, iron with beans, fish and meat, calcium with milk and small fish.

blocks.title: Water and fibre
blocks.md: **Water** is needed for blood, digestion, removing waste and keeping body temperature steady: drink clean, safe water. **Fibre** (from whole grains, fruits, vegetables, beans) is not digested but helps food move through the gut and helps prevent constipation.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Overcooking vegetables can destroy some vitamin C.
- Peeling and washing after cutting loses vitamins.
- Taking large doses of supplements is not a replacement for a varied diet; ask a health worker.
- Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Which foods in the market can give vitamin C?
steps: Fresh fruit and vegetables are the main source.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Why should vegetables not be boiled for a very long time?
steps: Some vitamins, such as vitamin C, are damaged by heat and dissolve in the water.
Cook briefly, use little water and use any cooking water in the sauce.

blocks.title: Balanced diet
blocks.md: A **balanced diet** contains all the nutrients in the right amounts for a person's age, sex, activity and health. It includes **energy foods** (staples), **body-building foods** (proteins), **protective foods** (fruit and vegetables) and enough water and fibre.

blocks.title: Plate idea
blocks.md: A simple guide: fill about **half the plate** with vegetables and fruit, about **a quarter** with starchy staple foods (cassava, plantain, maize, rice) and about **a quarter** with protein foods (fish, beans, eggs, meat), and use only a little oil, sugar and salt. These proportions are a general teaching guide, flagged for review.

blocks.caption: A single bar showing half vegetables and fruit, a quarter staple foods and a quarter protein foods.
blocks.alt: Stacked bar guide: 50 percent vegetables and fruit, 25 percent staple foods, 25 percent protein foods.

blocks.title: Planning a meal
blocks.md: 1. Choose a staple (e.g. fufu corn, plantain). 2. Add a protein (fish, beans, groundnuts). 3. Add a vegetable or fruit (eru, green leaves, tomatoes, mango). 4. Use little oil and salt. 5. Check cost and what is in season.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Different people need different amounts: children, pregnant women and manual workers have special needs.
- A cheap meal can still be balanced with beans, groundnuts and vegetables.
- Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Plan a balanced lunch with ndolé (a bitterleaf and groundnut dish) and plantain. What is missing?
steps: Ndolé is a leafy dish with groundnuts (and often fish or meat): protein and vegetable. Plantain is the staple (carbohydrate).
A fruit such as pawpaw or orange could be added for vitamin C.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A family has little money. Suggest a balanced and cheap dinner.
steps: Staple: maize or cassava. Protein: beans or groundnuts.
Vegetable: green leaves or tomato; use little oil.
